evidence.label: Goldfeld's analytic density conjecture and the 2-converse for elliptic curves
The mean analytic rank of quadratic twists of elliptic curves

headline: Among the quadratic twists of any elliptic curve, half are claimed to have analytic rank 0 and half rank 1.
scope: Every elliptic curve over the rationals; twists by squarefree integers d of both signs, ordered by the size of d.
plain: Twisting an elliptic curve by a number d gives a family of related curves. In 1979 Goldfeld conjectured that their average analytic rank is 1/2. The usual reading is that half have analytic rank 0, half have rank 1, and higher ranks are rare. These two papers claim both the half-and-half split and the average of 1/2, for every curve. The key new step claims that a small 2-power Selmer group forces the matching analytic rank.
doesNot: This does not decide the rank of every single twist, cover other orderings of twists, or give higher moments of analytic rank.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Dorian Goldfeld, the conjectured average rank of quadratic twists
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims Goldfeld's 1979 conjecture for every curve. Smith's Selmer statistics did much of the counting; the new step is a 2-converse.

explanation:
A whole number n is called congruent if it is the area of a right triangle with rational sides. The 3, 4, 5 triangle has area 6, so 6 is congruent. The triangle with sides 3/2, 20/3 and 41/6 has area 5. The triangle with sides 24/5, 35/12 and 337/60 has area 7. Fermat showed that 1 is not congruent. A classical fact links this to curves. The number n is congruent exactly when the curve y² = x³ − n²x has infinitely many rational points.

Those curves form one family. Start from the elliptic curve y² = x³ − x. Twisting it by n gives ny² = x³ − x, which is the same curve as y² = x³ − n²x after rescaling. In general, a quadratic twist of y² = x³ + ax + b by d is dy² = x³ + ax + b. The papers use every squarefree d, meaning no square larger than 1 divides it. Both positive and negative d count, ordered by size.

Each twist has a rank, the number of independent rational points that generate infinitely many others. It also has an analytic rank, the number of times its L-function vanishes at the centre. The L-function is built from point counts modulo every prime. The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture predicts the two ranks agree. A sign in the L-function's symmetry decides whether the analytic rank is even or odd.

In 1979, Goldfeld conjectured that the average analytic rank in such a family is 1/2. The density version says ranks 0 and 1 each occur half the time. For the congruent family, 1, 2 and 3 have rank 0, while 5, 6 and 7 have rank 1. Ranks of 2 or more should be rare enough to vanish in the average.

Earlier results gave only partial answers. In 1998, Ono and Skinner showed that many twists have nonzero central value, but not a positive share. Positive shares of both ranks were known for special curves, such as those with a rational 3-isogeny. Smith's 2025 preprint gives that Selmer coranks 0 and 1 each occur half the time, for every curve. A Selmer group is a computable group that bounds the rank. Smith's result for analytic ranks assumed the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.

The first paper fills that gap with a 2-converse. It claims that if the 2-power Selmer corank is 0 or 1, the analytic rank and the rank both equal it. It also claims the Tate–Shafarevich group, a group of hidden solutions, is finite. Combined with Smith's statistics, it claims ranks 0 and 1 each have density 1/2[2,5]. The rank and analytic rank then agree for almost every twist[4].

The second paper handles the average. A rare set of twists could still have huge ranks and pull the average up. The paper claims a bound on how much these rare high-rank twists can add. Together with the densities, the average analytic rank tends to 1/2[14]. The proof uses neither the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture nor the generalized Riemann hypothesis[15].

The hard step is going from the Selmer group to the L-function. The first paper builds finite families of twists indexed by strings of 0s and 1s. The curve under study sits at the all-zero string. Every other member is arranged to have the right analytic rank, with controlled 2-adic size. An interpolation argument then recovers the missing value at the all-zero string[16].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The density claim depends on Smith's preprint, and no specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the 2-converse and the tail estimate hold, along with Smith's Selmer statistics. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

claims.text: Twist parameters of both signs are counted together, ordered by absolute value.
claims.sourceLine: Thus positive and negative parameters are counted together and ordered by absolute value.

claims.text: For every curve, twists of analytic rank 0 and of rank 1 each have density 1/2.
claims.sourceLine: For every elliptic curve $E/\Q$ and each $j\in\{0,1\}$,

claims.text: Twists of analytic rank at least 2 have density zero.
claims.sourceLine: Consequently the twists of analytic rank at least two have density zero.

claims.text: For almost every twist the two ranks agree and Sha is finite.
claims.sourceLine: For a density-one set of signed squarefree parameters $d$, the analytic and Mordell--Weil ranks of $E^{(d)}$ agree and its whole Tate--Shafarevich group is finite.

claims.text: The density theorem combines the 2-converse with Smith's Selmer distribution.
claims.sourceLine: The theorem follows by combining the pointwise $2$-converse with Smith's distribution of full $2$-power Selmer coranks

claims.text: The main work is the pointwise converse.
claims.sourceLine: The main work of this paper is the pointwise converse.

claims.text: There is no restriction on reduction type, CM, torsion or isogenies.
claims.sourceLine: There is no restriction on reduction type, complex multiplication, rational torsion, or rational isogenies.

claims.text: Goldfeld's 1979 formulation asks for the mean analytic order.
claims.sourceLine: Goldfeld's original 1979 formulation asks for the mean analytic order in a family parametrized by quadratic-field discriminants

claims.text: The density form predicts ranks 0 and 1 each half the time.
claims.sourceLine: The density formulation predicts that analytic ranks zero and one each occur half the time.

claims.text: Ono and Skinner gave a lower bound of order X/log X for nonvanishing twists.
claims.sourceLine: Ono--Skinner obtained a lower bound of order $X/\log X$ for the number of nonvanishing central values among twists by fundamental discriminants $D$ with $0<|D|\le X$

claims.text: Kriz and Li proved both positive proportions for curves with a rational 3-isogeny.
claims.sourceLine: Kriz--Li proved both positive proportions for every rational elliptic curve admitting a rational $3$-isogeny

claims.text: Rare high-rank twists can still affect the mean.
claims.sourceLine: A zero-density exceptional family can still contribute to a rank-weighted average.

claims.text: The average analytic rank of the twists tends to 1/2.
claims.sourceLine: we prove that the average analytic rank of its quadratic twists tends to \(1/2\) when signed squarefree twist parameters are ordered by absolute value.

claims.text: The mean proof uses neither BSD nor GRH.
claims.sourceLine: The proof invokes neither the Birch--Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture nor the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
